blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 19 (Chromosome and DNA), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Who discovered chromosomes and who gave them their name?
blocks.explanation: Chromosomes were discovered by the German embryologist Walther Flemming in 1882 in the rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae. The name "chromosome" (coloured bodies) was proposed by the German anatomist Waldeyer-Hartz in 1888.

book_ref.quote: He discovered chromosomes in the rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae

blocks.prompt: 2 What is a karyotype? How do somatic cells and gametes differ in chromosomes?
blocks.explanation: Karyotype is the complete set of chromosomes of a species, with its own number and shape. In somatic cells of diploid organisms chromosomes occur in homologous pairs; gametes have half the number and their chromosomes are not in pairs.

book_ref.quote: The number and shape of chromosomes are different in each species

blocks.prompt: 3 How does chromatin change into chromosomes when a cell prepares to divide?
blocks.explanation: The DNA starts to coil and wraps around small units of histones. These units coil further into a highly condensed form; with more coiling the structure becomes thicker and shorter and finally forms compact thread-like chromosomes.

book_ref.quote: When a cell prepares to divide, the DNA starts to coil

blocks.prompt: 4 What are sister chromatids? Where are they joined?
blocks.explanation: After duplication of chromatin in interphase, each chromosome consists of two identical strands called sister chromatids. They are attached to each other at a constricted region called the centromere.

book_ref.quote: They are attached to each other at a constricted region called the centromere

blocks.prompt: 5 What is a kinetochore? Write its function.
blocks.explanation: The kinetochore is a disc-shaped protein structure attached to the centromere. It serves as the point where chromosomes attach to the mitotic spindle during cell division.

book_ref.quote: It serves as the point where chromosomes attach to the mitotic spindle

blocks.prompt: 6 What is secondary constriction? What is its function?
blocks.explanation: In some chromosomes there is another constriction besides the centromere, called secondary constriction or Nuclear Organizer Region (NOR). It makes nucleoli during interphase.

book_ref.quote: In some chromosomes, there may be another constriction

blocks.prompt: 7 What is a satellite of a chromosome? What is junk DNA?
blocks.explanation: The knob-like end of a chromosome beside the secondary constriction is called the satellite. This region has highly repetitive DNA sequences called junk DNA.

book_ref.quote: This region has highly repetitive DNA sequences called junk DNA

blocks.prompt: 8 What are telomeres? Why are they important?
blocks.explanation: Telomeres are the terminal ends of chromosomes. They prevent two chromosomes from attaching with each other at their ends.

book_ref.quote: They prevent the two chromosomes to attach with each other from their ends

blocks.prompt: 9 Differentiate between metacentric and acrocentric chromosomes.
blocks.explanation: They differ in the position of the centromere.

book_ref.quote: The chromosomes in which centromere is at the centre are called metacentric chromosomes

rows: Centromere is at the centre
Centromere is located near the end

blocks.text: 19.1.2 Chemical Composition and Organization of Chromosome

blocks.prompt: 10 Why does DNA bind strongly to histone proteins?
blocks.explanation: DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate groups, while histones are positively charged due to the abundance of basic amino acids such as arginine and lysine. So DNA has strong affinity to histones.

book_ref.quote: It has strong affinity to histone proteins

blocks.prompt: 11 What is a nucleosome? Name the histones of its octamer.
blocks.explanation: A nucleosome is an aggregation formed when about 146 nucleotides of DNA wrap twice around a histone octamer. The octamer is a set of 8 histones: two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.

book_ref.quote: set of 8 histone molecules i.e., two copies each of the histones

blocks.prompt: 12 What are linker DNA and linker histone?
blocks.explanation: Linker DNA is the stretch of about 80 nucleotides that connects nucleosomes. The linker histone, H1 (the fifth type of histone), is present at the base of the nucleosome near the DNA entry and exit points and helps in the winding of the chain of nucleosomes.

book_ref.quote: It helps in the winding of the chain of nucleosomes

blocks.prompt: 13 Differentiate between nucleosome string and chromatin fibre.
blocks.explanation: Both are levels of chromosome organization; the chromatin fibre is formed by further coiling of the nucleosome string.

book_ref.quote: the nucleosome string again coils about its axis

rows: Nucleosomes (without linker histone) arranged like beads on a string
Tightly packed (condensed) nucleosomes
11 nm thick
30 nm thick
Formed after replication when DNA wraps around histone octamers
Formed in early stages of cell division when the nucleosome string coils again about its axis

blocks.prompt: 14 What is a supercoil? How is a chromatid formed from it?
blocks.explanation: The chromatin fibre folds upon itself to make a supercoil, 300 nm thick. The supercoil further coils and condenses and takes the shape of a chromatid, 700 nm thick.

book_ref.quote: The supercoil further coils and condenses

blocks.text: 19.1.3 The Concept of Genes and Alleles

blocks.prompt: 15 Give an example to show that alleles lie at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
blocks.explanation: If a chromosome has the allele for eye colour at a particular locus, its homologous chromosome will carry the allele of the same character (eye colour) at the same locus.

book_ref.quote: if a chromosome has the allele for

blocks.prompt: 16 Which facts had been confirmed before scientists asked whether genes are made of DNA or protein?
blocks.explanation:
1. Genes are the units of inheritance.
2. Genes are located on chromosomes.
3. Chromosomes are made of DNA and proteins.

book_ref.quote: Genes are located on chromosomes, and

blocks.prompt: 17 List the characteristics a molecule must have to serve as genetic material.
blocks.explanation:
1. It must code for the sequence of amino acids in proteins.
2. It must replicate itself prior to cell division.
3. It must be in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
4. It must be able to change over time to account for evolution.
Only DNA fulfils all these.

book_ref.quote: A molecule that serves as genetic material must have certain characteristics

blocks.prompt: 18 Differentiate between the S-type and R-type strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
blocks.explanation: The two strains differ in coat, colony and effect on mice.

book_ref.quote: strain lacked polysaccharide coat and forms a

rows: Has a polysaccharide coat
Lacks polysaccharide coat
Forms a smooth colony
Forms a rough colony
Virulent: injected mice developed pneumonia and died
Non-virulent: injected mice showed no effects

blocks.prompt: 19 What did Griffith think was the cause of the virulence of S-type bacteria?
blocks.explanation: Griffith thought that the virulent effect of S-type might be due to its polysaccharide coat, which protects it from the host's immune system.

book_ref.quote: Griffith thought that the virulent effect of S-type might be due to its polysaccharide coat

blocks.prompt: 20 What is transformation? What did Griffith conclude from it?
blocks.explanation: Transformation is the transfer of genetic material from one organism to another to change the genetic makeup of the recipient. Griffith concluded that the information for the polysaccharide coat and virulence passed from heat-killed S-type to live R-type, which became virulent S-type.

book_ref.quote: the transfer of genetic material from one organism to another

blocks.prompt: 21 How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty show that proteins are not the transforming principle?
blocks.explanation: They removed proteins from dead S-type bacteria and mixed them with live R-type. Mice injected with this mixture developed disease and live S-type bacteria were found in them. So transformation still occurred without proteins.

book_ref.quote: It means that proteins are not responsible for transforming R-type into S-type

blocks.prompt: 22 What are bacteriophages? What happens when a lytic bacteriophage infects a bacterium?
blocks.explanation: Bacteriophages are viruses that attack bacteria; they consist of a core (DNA or RNA) and a protein coat. A lytic phage binds to the bacterial surface and injects material that directs the production of new phages; the cell finally lyses and new phages are released.

book_ref.quote: Bacteriophages consist of a core (made of DNA or RNA) and a protein coat

blocks.prompt: 23 How did Hershey and Chase label the protein and the DNA of bacteriophages separately?
blocks.explanation: Some phages were grown on a medium with ³⁵S; it was incorporated into the amino acids of the protein coats. Other phages were grown with ³²P; it was incorporated into the phosphate groups of the DNA.

book_ref.quote: Some bacteriophages were grown on a medium containing an isotope of sulphur

blocks.prompt: 24 Differentiate between the results of setup 1 and setup 2 of the Hershey-Chase experiment.
blocks.explanation: The two setups used differently labelled bacteriophages.

book_ref.quote: radioactivity was observed in bacterial cells and not in the medium

rows: Bacteriophages with ³⁵S labelled protein
Bacteriophages with ³²P labelled DNA
Radioactivity found in the medium, not in bacterial cells
Radioactivity found in bacterial cells, not in the medium
Shows the protein coat remained outside
Shows DNA entered the cells and directed new phages

blocks.prompt: 25 Define DNA replication. When does it take place?
blocks.explanation: DNA replication is the process in which a DNA molecule makes its identical copy (replica); as DNA is double-stranded it copies both strands. It happens before a cell divides, during the S-phase of interphase.

book_ref.quote: DNA replication is the process in which the molecule of DNA makes its identical copy

blocks.text: 19.3.1 Models Proposed for the Mechanism of DNA Replication

blocks.prompt: 26 Differentiate between the semi-conservative and dispersive models of DNA replication.
blocks.explanation: Both models break the parent double helix, but in different ways.

book_ref.quote: Each of these strands acts as a template for the synthesis of a new strand

rows: The two parent strands separate
Parent DNA is broken and dispersed into nucleotides
Each parent strand acts as a template for a new strand
Old nucleotides combine with new nucleotides to make the four strands
Each daughter DNA has one parent strand and one new strand
Both daughter DNAs have strands that are mixtures of old and new nucleotides

blocks.prompt: 27 Why did Meselson and Stahl transfer the ¹⁵N bacteria to a ¹⁴N medium?
blocks.explanation: After many generations in ¹⁵N the bacterial DNA was denser than normal. In the ¹⁴N medium the bacteria would make new DNA using ¹⁴N, so old (heavy) and new (light) strands could be told apart by density.

book_ref.quote: Then, they transferred the new bacteria

blocks.prompt: 28 How were heavy and light DNAs separated in the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
blocks.explanation: The DNA was dissolved in aqueous cesium chloride and ultracentrifuged. This created a cesium density gradient (denser cesium at the bottom); each DNA settled where its density matched the cesium, so ¹⁵N DNA went further down than ¹⁴N DNA.

book_ref.quote: The ultracentrifugation created a gradient of cesium density

blocks.prompt: 29 What is a pulse-chase experiment? Name its two stages.
blocks.explanation: It is an experiment in which radio-isotope labelled DNA is traced in the progeny of an organism. Pulse stage: the organism is briefly exposed to the radio-isotope and incorporates it into DNA. Chase stage: the labelled DNA is observed over time by measuring its radioactivity.

book_ref.quote: An experiment in which a radio-isotope labelled DNA is traced in the progeny

blocks.prompt: 30 Differentiate between the DNA collected at 0 minutes and at 20 minutes in the Meselson-Stahl experiment.
blocks.explanation: The two samples differ in density and strand make-up.

book_ref.quote: DNA collected before any replication was heaviest

rows: Collected before any replication
Collected after the first replication in ¹⁴N medium
Heaviest: a single band of heavy density
A single band of intermediate density
Both strands made of ¹⁵N
Hybrid: one ¹⁴N strand and one ¹⁵N strand

blocks.prompt: 31 What is a replication origin site? How many are there in prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
blocks.explanation: It is a specific sequence of nucleotides on DNA where replication begins. Prokaryotes have only one replication origin site; eukaryotes have many along the length of DNA.

book_ref.quote: where there is a specific sequence of nucleotides called a replication origin site

blocks.prompt: 32 Why are supercoils produced during replication and how are they prevented?
blocks.explanation: Unwinding of the DNA helix by helicases produces supercoils ahead of the replication fork. The enzyme gyrase (topoisomerase) attaches ahead of the fork and prevents supercoiling.

book_ref.quote: Due to unwinding of the DNA helix, supercoils are produced

blocks.prompt: 33 What is a primer? Why is it needed in DNA replication?
blocks.explanation: A primer is a short fragment of 5-10 RNA nucleotides attached by the enzyme primase in front of each template strand at the origin. It is needed because new DNA cannot be formed on exposed strands unless some nucleotides are already arranged on the template.

book_ref.quote: an enzyme primase attaches some RNA nucleotides

blocks.prompt: 34 Name the raw materials of DNA synthesis. How do they provide energy?
blocks.explanation: The raw materials are deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates: dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP, each with three phosphate groups. As DNA polymerase III attaches a nucleotide, it breaks off two phosphates; this releases energy for the building process.

book_ref.quote: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP)

blocks.prompt: 35 What are Okazaki fragments? Why is each one given a new primer?
blocks.explanation: Okazaki fragments are short, separate pieces of DNA made on the lagging strand, which grows discontinuously away from the fork. As the DNA unzips further, the enzyme has to jump back to a new primer to start each new segment.

book_ref.quote: It makes short, separate pieces of DNA called Okazaki fragments

blocks.prompt: 36 What are termination site and replicon?
blocks.explanation: The termination site is the specific nucleotide sequence where replication terminates. The region of DNA between the origin site and the termination site is a replication unit or replicon.

book_ref.quote: The termination of replication occurs at specific sequence of nucleotides called termination site

blocks.prompt: 37 What part of the parent DNA is conserved in each daughter DNA?
blocks.explanation: During replication one strand of the original DNA is conserved while the daughter strand is made anew. So half of the original DNA molecule is conserved in each new generation of DNA.

book_ref.quote: half of the original DNA molecule is conserved in each new generation of DNA

blocks.prompt: 38 Differentiate between DNA replication in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
blocks.explanation: They differ in site, enzymes, origin/termination sites and Okazaki fragments.

book_ref.quote: In prokaryotes, replication occurs in the cytoplasm

rows: Occurs in the cytoplasm (no nucleus)
Occurs in the nucleus
DNA polymerase I, II and III work
At least 14 polymerases (e.g. alpha, delta, epsilon)
Single origin and single termination site
Multiple origin and termination sites on each chromosome; several replicons
Okazaki fragments longer (1000-2000 nucleotides)
Okazaki fragments short (100-200 nucleotides)

blocks.prompt: 39 How do eukaryotes replicate their massive amount of DNA in time?
blocks.explanation: Eukaryotes have massive amounts of linear DNA. To compensate, they start replication at thousands of different origin sites along a single chromosome at the same time.

book_ref.quote: eukaryotes start replication at thousands of different origin sites

blocks.prompt: 40 Give two uses of DNA replication in biotechnology other than PCR.
blocks.explanation:
1. Recombinant DNA technology: DNA cut from different sources is replicated to amplify it.
2. Genome sequencing: replication makes multiple copies of the genome to be sequenced.
(Also diagnostic studies: specific sections of a patient's DNA are replicated and searched for mutations.)

book_ref.quote: In genome sequencing, scientists use DNA replication

blocks.prompt: 41 Differentiate between stability and variability of DNA.
blocks.explanation: Both are properties of replicating DNA.

book_ref.quote: While stability is the rule

rows: Ability of DNA to be copied with accuracy
A permanent change in DNA sequence (mutation)
Is the rule; maintained by proofreading of DNA polymerase III
Is an exception; caused by replication errors or environmental factors
Maintains the specific traits of an organism
Primary source of new traits; raw material for evolution

blocks.prompt: 42 What is meant by gene expression?
blocks.explanation: A gene is a specific sequence of nucleotides on DNA that directs the synthesis of a polypeptide. A gene expresses itself by making a protein or an enzyme that controls the development of a specific trait.

book_ref.quote: a gene expresses itself by making a protein or an enzyme

blocks.prompt: 43 Which questions arose about the genetic code after the discovery of DNA structure and central dogma?
blocks.explanation:
1. How can DNA, with only four nucleotides, store information for thousands of specific proteins?
2. What is the nature of the genetic code?
3. How does the order of nucleotides specify the order of amino acids in a polypeptide?

book_ref.quote: How can DNA, a substance containing only four different nucleotides

blocks.prompt: 44 Why did Crick conclude that a codon must have three nucleotides?
blocks.explanation: Single nucleotides could code only 4 amino acids and pairs only 16 (4 × 4), fewer than the 20 amino acids. Triplets give 64 (4 × 4 × 4) combinations, more than enough for 20 amino acids.

book_ref.quote: They reached to a conclusion that one codon should be a sequence of 3 nucleotides

blocks.prompt: 45 Describe Nirenberg's poly-U experiment and its result.
blocks.explanation: In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg made a poly-U mRNA (uracil nucleotides only) and added it to the cytoplasm of bacteria. The bacteria produced a polypeptide of many phenylalanines, so he concluded that the codon UUU specifies phenylalanine.

book_ref.quote: In 1961, the American biochemist, Marshall Nirenberg made a poly-U mRNA

blocks.prompt: 46 Who shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology & Medicine and for what work?
blocks.explanation: Nirenberg for work on the genetic code, Har Gobind Khorana for the synthesis of nucleic acids, and Robert Holley for discovering the chemical structure of transfer-RNA.

book_ref.quote: The 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology

blocks.prompt: 47 What is meant by universality of the genetic code? Give an exception.
blocks.explanation: The genetic code is the same in almost all organisms, e.g. AGA specifies arginine in bacteria, humans and all others; so genes can be transferred among organisms. Exception: the code in mitochondrial DNA is slightly different (also some ciliates and viruses).

book_ref.quote: The genetic code is same in almost all organisms

blocks.prompt: 48 What is meant by the genetic code being non-overlapping? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Each triplet codon is read independently of the adjacent codons. For example, AUGAGCGCA is read only as AUG/AGC/GCA, never as AUG/UGA/GAG.

book_ref.quote: each triplet codon is read independently of the adjacent codons

blocks.prompt: 49 Differentiate between the template strand and the coding strand of DNA.
blocks.explanation: Only one of the two DNA strands is transcribed.

book_ref.quote: Only one strand of DNA, called the template strand, is transcribed

rows: Is transcribed
Is not transcribed
mRNA is complementary to it
Has the same sequence as the mRNA, except T in place of U
Also called antisense (–) strand
Also called sense (+) strand

blocks.prompt: 50 What is a promoter? Is it transcribed?
blocks.explanation: A promoter is a special nucleotide sequence on template DNA to which RNA polymerase binds to start transcription. It is not itself transcribed by the enzyme.

book_ref.quote: This sequence is called promoter

blocks.prompt: 51 Differentiate between the promoters of prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
blocks.explanation: Both have two promoters at fixed distances before the start point of the gene.

book_ref.quote: In prokaryotes, a promoter TTGACA is present 35 nucleotides before the start point of gene

rows: TTGACA, 35 nucleotides before the start point (–35 sequence)
TATAAA (TATA box), 25 nucleotides before the start point (–25 sequence)
TATAAT, 10 nucleotides before the start point (–10 sequence)
GGCCAATCT (CAAT box), 70 nucleotides before the start point (–70 sequence)

blocks.prompt: 52 Name the RNA polymerases of eukaryotes and the RNA each makes.
blocks.explanation: RNA polymerase I makes rRNA in the nucleolus; RNA polymerase II makes mRNA; RNA polymerase III makes tRNA. (Prokaryotes have only one RNA polymerase for all three kinds.)

book_ref.quote: Eukaryotes have three different RNA polymerases

blocks.prompt: 53 What is a transcription bubble? How is it formed?
blocks.explanation: When RNA polymerase attaches to the promoter its σ subunit is removed; the other four subunits (core enzyme) unwind the DNA and break the base-pairs. This forms a bubble-like structure, the transcription bubble, in which the RNA chain is assembled.

book_ref.quote: It results in the formation of a bubble-like structure

blocks.prompt: 54 What is a GC hairpin? How does it help to end transcription?
blocks.explanation: When the GC pairs of the stop region are transcribed, hydrogen bonds form within the mRNA strand, creating a loop called the GC hairpin with a tail of four or more U. It makes RNA polymerase pause; the weak U-A pairing cannot hold the hybrid, so RNA dissociates and transcription stops.

book_ref.quote: This intra-strand nucleotide-pairing (base-pairing) creates a loop

blocks.prompt: 55 Differentiate between the 5′ cap and the 3′ poly-A tail of mRNA.
blocks.explanation: Both are added to eukaryotic mRNA before it leaves the nucleus.

book_ref.quote: It protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases during its journey

rows: Added at the 5′ end of mRNA
Added at the 3′ end of mRNA
A methylated GTP joined 5′ to 5′ with the terminal A or G
A small chain of about 250 A nucleotides
Protects mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases
Protects the transcript from degradation by nucleases

blocks.prompt: 56 Why does prokaryotic mRNA not undergo post-transcriptional modification?
blocks.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus and transcription happens in the cytoplasm, so their new mRNA does not need to travel anywhere to start translation. In eukaryotes the mRNA must travel from nucleus to cytoplasm, so it is modified for the journey.

book_ref.quote: As the prokaryotes have no nucleus and transcription happens in cytoplasm

blocks.prompt: 57 What is meant by activation of amino acids?
blocks.explanation: Before protein synthesis, specific tRNAs attach with specific amino acids to make aminoacyl-tRNAs (aa-tRNA). The enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (20 kinds) does this; the aa-tRNA delivers the amino acid to the ribosome.

book_ref.quote: Specific tRNAs attach with specific amino acids and make aminoacyl-tRNAs

blocks.prompt: 58 Differentiate between the P site and the A site of a ribosome.
blocks.explanation: Both are sites of the ribosome used in translation.

book_ref.quote: where peptide bonds will form between amino acids

rows: Where peptide bonds form between amino acids
Where the next aa-tRNA binds
Holds the first aa-tRNA in the initiation complex
Exposes the next codon of mRNA
Holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain after translocation
Receives the release factor when a stop codon arrives

blocks.prompt: 59 What are the roles of initiation factors in translation?
blocks.explanation: One initiation factor controls the binding of the aa-tRNA carrying the first amino acid to the smaller ribosomal subunit. Another attaches the 5′ end of mRNA with the smaller subunit and positions the anticodon of aa-tRNA over the first codon (AUG).

book_ref.quote: Another initiation factor attaches the 5

blocks.prompt: 60 What is translocation during translation? What is its result?
blocks.explanation: Translocation is the movement of the ribosome three nucleotides along the mRNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction. As a result the aa-tRNA with the peptide chain shifts from the A site to the P site, a new codon is exposed at the A site and the empty tRNA moves to the E site to leave.

book_ref.quote: The ribosome moves three nucleotides along the mRNA

blocks.prompt: 61 How is translation terminated?
blocks.explanation: When a stop codon reaches the A site no aa-tRNA comes, as stop codons have no anticodon. A release factor protein recognizes it and releases the polypeptide from the tRNA at the P site; the tRNA is released and the ribosomal subunits separate from mRNA.

book_ref.quote: It releases the polypeptide from the tRNA present at P site

blocks.prompt: 62 Why do different cell types of an organism make different proteins though their genome is the same?
blocks.explanation: All genes are not turned ON in all cells; specific genes are turned ON in each cell type, and different genes are expressed at different times. Regulator proteins control this turning ON and OFF.

book_ref.quote: all types of cells contain the same genome

blocks.prompt: 63 Name the levels at which gene expression is regulated.
blocks.explanation:
1. Transcriptional level: rate of transcription.
2. Post-transcriptional level: modification of mRNA.
3. Translational level: rate of translation.
4. Post-translational level: modification of protein (folding, stability).

book_ref.quote: Regulation of gene expressions occurs at several levels

blocks.prompt: 64 How can genes be regulated during splicing?
blocks.explanation: In eukaryotes, specific regulatory proteins in specific cell types control splicing; they remove introns or exons in different ways. So mRNAs of different lengths are made and more than one polypeptide is produced from a single gene.

book_ref.quote: Specific regulatory proteins in specific cell types control splicing

blocks.prompt: 65 Give an example of a gene that is expressed in one cell type but turned OFF in another.
blocks.explanation: Liver cells express the genes for the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, which breaks alcohol down into non-toxic molecules. Brain neurons also have these genes but keep them unexpressed (turned OFF).

book_ref.quote: This enzyme breaks alcohol down into a non-toxic molecules

blocks.prompt: 66 Differentiate between natural and induced mutations.
blocks.explanation: They differ in cause and effect.

book_ref.quote: Natural mutations occur spontaneously as a result of sequencing errors

rows: Occur spontaneously
Caused by external factors
Due to sequencing errors or DNA damage during replication
Due to mutagens, radiation, environmental chemicals (pesticides, pollutants) or treatments like chemotherapy
Part of evolution; may be beneficial, neutral or harmful
Can have serious health effects

blocks.prompt: 67 Differentiate between a mutagen and a mutant.
blocks.explanation: One causes mutation; the other carries it.

book_ref.quote: The agents that cause mutations are called mutagens

rows: An agent that causes mutation
The organism or cell in which mutation occurs
e.g. radiation or mutagen chemicals such as mustard gas
e.g. a cell whose DNA sequence has changed

blocks.prompt: 68 How do mutations contribute to evolution?
blocks.explanation: Mutation and recombination create new DNA sequences (alleles) and combinations of alleles. These form new traits that may be advantageous, harmful or neutral; natural selection acts on them and the frequencies of advantageous alleles increase, leading to evolution in the long run.

book_ref.quote: Natural selection acts upon the variations created by new traits

blocks.prompt: 69 Differentiate between insertion and deletion mutations.
blocks.explanation: Both are point mutations that change the number of nucleotides.

book_ref.quote: It is the addition of one or more extra nucleotides into the DNA

rows: Adds one or more extra nucleotides into DNA
Removes one or more nucleotides from DNA
Usually due to errors during replication
e.g. deletion of three nucleotides in cystic fibrosis

blocks.prompt: 70 What is a gene mutation? Which is its most common type?
blocks.explanation: Gene mutation is a general term for any change within the chemical structure of a single gene; it is a change at the molecular (nucleotide sequence) level rather than the chromosomal level. Point mutations are the most common gene mutations.

book_ref.quote: Gene mutation is a general term for any change within the chemical structure

blocks.prompt: 71 How do mutagen chemicals cause point mutations?
blocks.explanation: Some resemble nucleotides and are incorporated into DNA, which then cannot be properly transcribed. Some remove the amino group from adenine or cytosine, causing mis-pairing. Some add hydrocarbon groups to nucleotides, also causing mis-pairing.

book_ref.quote: Some chemicals remove the amino group from adenine or cytosine

blocks.prompt: 72 How do spontaneous point mutations occur?
blocks.explanation: Sometimes nucleotides spontaneously shift to alternative positions and DNA polymerase pairs a different nucleotide with them during replication. Sometimes sequences misalign when homologous chromosomes pair; a loop forms and is cut out, deleting several hundred nucleotides.

book_ref.quote: Sometimes nucleotides spontaneously shift to alternative positions

blocks.prompt: 73 Differentiate between silent and missense mutations.
blocks.explanation: Both are minor mutations; they differ in their effect on the protein.

book_ref.quote: These mutations change only one amino acid

rows: Does not change the amino acid sequence of the protein
Changes one amino acid, which can affect protein function
Possible because of degeneracy of the code
The new codon specifies a different amino acid
e.g. mRNA codon GGC to GGU: both give glycine
e.g. haemoglobin gene: glutamic acid replaced by valine (sickle cell anaemia)

blocks.prompt: 74 Why are most mutations harmful? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Most mutations disrupt the normal functioning of genes. A change of a single amino acid in haemoglobin causes sickle cell anaemia; mutations disrupting gene regulation can contribute to cancer; some give non-functional proteins, e.g. phenylketonuria.

book_ref.quote: Most mutations disrupt the normal functioning of genes

blocks.prompt: 75 How does the point mutation of sickle cell anaemia affect the red blood cells?
blocks.explanation: A child with both recessive alleles makes abnormal β chains with glutamic acid replaced by valine. The abnormal haemoglobin carries less oxygen than normal and the RBCs become sickle shaped.

book_ref.quote: The abnormal haemoglobin carries less than normal oxygen

blocks.prompt: 76 How is phenylketonuria managed?
blocks.explanation: Patients avoid foods high in phenylalanine (meat, dairy products, eggs, some grains); blood phenylalanine is monitored regularly to adjust the diet; nutritional supplements provide the vitamins and minerals lacking in the low-phenylalanine diet.

book_ref.quote: Individuals with PKU have to avoid foods that are high in phenylalanine

blocks.prompt: 77 What are gene therapy and pharmacogenomics?
blocks.explanation: Gene therapy corrects or replaces the mutated gene with a functional gene. Pharmacogenomics tailors drug treatment to an individual's genetic makeup: by analysing a patient's DNA, doctors can identify the best drug.

book_ref.quote: It involves correcting or replacing the mutated gene with a functional gene

blocks.prompt: 78 What is genetic counselling?
blocks.explanation: For people with a family history of genetic diseases, genetic counselling provides information and support. It includes genetic testing, education on the disease, and guidance on family planning and reproductive options.

book_ref.quote: For individuals with a family history of genetic diseases

blocks.prompt: 79 Differentiate between translocation and inversion.
blocks.explanation: Both are chromosomal rearrangements, usually caused by breakage of DNA at two locations.

book_ref.quote: In translocations, a segment of one chromosome becomes part of another chromosome

rows: A segment of one chromosome becomes part of another chromosome
The orientation of a portion of a chromosome is reversed
Involves two chromosomes
Occurs within one chromosome

blocks.prompt: 80 What is insertional inactivation? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Transposons (jumping genes) move at random in the genome; some get inserted into genes and inactivate them. E.g. a human transposon inserted into the clotting factor IX gene on the X chromosome places a stop codon in the gene, causing X-linked haemophilia.

book_ref.quote: Some transposons are able to be inserted into genes and inactivate the genes

blocks.prompt: 81 Why is the age of the mother more critical than that of the father for non-disjunction?
blocks.explanation: All future eggs reach prophase I by the time a female is born, so her eggs are as old as she is and non-disjunction can accumulate in them. Men produce new sperm daily.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, the age of mother is more critical than that of father

blocks.prompt: 82 Differentiate between Down syndrome and Turner syndrome.
blocks.explanation: Both arise from non-disjunction but differ in the chromosomes involved.

blocks.prompt: 83 What is triple X syndrome? Give its features.
blocks.explanation: If an XX egg fuses with an X sperm, the female child has 47 chromosomes with XXX sex chromosomes (trisomy X). Such females show learning disabilities, tall stature and wide-spaced eyes; they are fertile and puberty starts at normal age.

blocks.prompt: 84 How can non-disjunction in the father produce Klinefelter syndrome?
blocks.explanation: Non-disjunction during gamete formation in the father can give a sperm with both X and Y chromosomes (XY). If this sperm fertilizes a normal X egg, the child has XXY chromosomes: Klinefelter syndrome.

book_ref.quote: Such non-disjunction may also occur in father during gamete formation

blocks.prompt: 85 Why are individuals with an extra chromosome 21 or 22 generally short with poor muscles?
blocks.explanation: Such individuals usually survive to adulthood, but the maturation of their skeletal system is delayed, so they are generally short and have poor muscles; their mental development is also affected.

book_ref.quote: the maturation of the skeletal system is delayed
